title: $709 from 2,430 paper trades, and it spent part of September under water. What would a bot need to show you before you trusted it?
author: QuanTradin
selftext:
Saw the thread this week about 11 strategies over 8 years where none beat buy and hold, and the one about splitting $10k across 52 mediocre bots. This is the other side of that argument: one small, boring bot off my own paper desk, card and all.

The rule in one sentence: on 1-minute bars, short a US stock that is already down 10% over 60 days, sits near its 52-week low, gets rejected at its 20 EMA, and has sellers in control (-DI over +DI) on 1.5x normal volume.

What the card shows, 25 Aug to 23 Oct: +$709.11 realized over 2,430 trades, 51.1% of them winners, best run 24 in a row. Look at the curve though. It drifted up for two weeks, fell below zero in mid September and stayed there for a while, climbed to its best point in mid October, then gave a good chunk of that back in the last week.

The doubt: that is well under a dollar a trade. A slightly worse fill on each one and the whole thing is flat. Two months is also nowhere near enough to know if the September hole is the normal bad patch or a small version of a worse one.

So the question for this room, since half of you are running bots right now: what would a card like this have to show before you'd let it near a real account? Longer history, a cost per trade, a max drawdown number, something else?

How Quantradin helps with this: I built Quantradin so a rule like this one can be written in plain words, replayed over years of past American stock and option prices with no peeking ahead, and then left running as a fake-money bot that prints this card for itself. It covers American equities and their option chains, no crypto, no gold, and it's free. [quantradin.com](http://quantradin.com)

Paper money, simulated, not advice. No promise about what it does next.

comments.author: Infamous_Food_3766
comments.body: how are u handling stocks that weren't available to short at the time? would be useful to see rejected signals beside filled trades, plus whether borrow costs are included in that $709. the entry rules are clear, just curious how that side of the paper model works.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: fair hole to poke. borrow is a flat modelled charge, not that stock's real rate on that day, and nothing checks whether shares were actually there to short, so a hard-to-borrow name fills like any other. the charge is inside the $709. rejected signals next to the fills is a good ask, writing it down.

comments.author: investigatormaker
comments.body:
Three things I'd want on the card. A cost stress: rerun with a fixed adverse fill on every trade and show where the curve goes flat, since you already doubt the edge per trade. Drawdown by duration, meaning how many days September stayed under water. And because these are shorts on stocks near 52-week lows, whether borrow was available at the fill; paper desks often assume every short is shortable at the touch.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: the borrow one I can answer: it's a flat modelled charge, nothing checks whether shares were actually there to short, so a hard-to-borrow name fills like any other. that flatters a 52-week-low short list and I'd rather say so than hide it. the adverse-fill rerun and days under water I don't have to hand, so I'm not going to guess them here.
